script: In 1941, British intelligence had a problem. They needed brilliant minds to crack the Nazi Enigma code, but they couldn't exactly advertise for spies. So they came up with a strange plan. The Daily Telegraph newspaper ran a public crossword contest, timing the fastest readers who could solve it in under twelve minutes. What the contestants didn't know was that intelligence officers were secretly watching the results. Anyone who finished fast enough got a mysterious letter inviting them to a quiet manor house called Bletchley Park, for, quote, work of national importance. Many of the recruits had no idea they had just been hired as codebreakers until they arrived. Those same puzzle solvers went on to break Enigma, an achievement historians say shortened the war by two years.
